related_questions.question: Why did blacklisted union members have trouble finding jobs after the Pullman Strike?

text_blocks.snippet: Following the Pullman Strike, blacklisted union members struggled to find jobs because employers viewed them as "troublemakers" and were hesitant to hire individuals associated with labor unrest. This perception was reinforced by the circulation of their names on "blacklists" among employers, discouraging them from offering employment.
snippet_highlighted_words: employers viewed them as "troublemakers" and were hesitant to hire individuals associated with labor unrest

list.title: Perception as troublemakers:
list.snippet: Employers feared that hiring union members who had participated in the strike would disrupt their operations and lead to further conflict.

list.title: Blacklisting:
list.snippet: The practice of circulating names of striking workers among employers created a barrier to re-employment, as companies were hesitant to hire individuals perceived as disruptive.

list.title: General anti-union sentiment:
list.snippet: The aftermath of the Pullman Strike saw strong anti-union sentiment, with employers often siding with management and prioritizing stability over workers' rights.

list.title: Consequences of the strike:
list.snippet: The strike's failure and subsequent federal intervention, including the imprisonment of some union leaders like Eugene Debs, further solidified the negative perception of union involvement.

list.title: Limited job opportunities:
list.snippet: The combination of these factors significantly limited the employment opportunities for blacklisted workers, making it difficult for them to re-enter the workforce and impacting their economic well-being.
